title: Can the sum of two angles give a rule for a triangle?
description: The video adds the pairs that work and the pairs that fail from the last question, and compares the sums with one hundred and eighty degrees. This gives a rule for two angles, which is checked with the angles sixty and seventy from the book.
teaching_notes: One idea: two angles make a triangle when each is more than zero and their sum is less than one hundred and eighty degrees. Watch for students who forget the condition that each angle is more than zero.

source: Like the triangle inequality, can you form a rule that describes the two angles for which a triangle is possible? Can the sum of the two angles be used for framing this rule?
video_script.why: The child has sorted pairs of angles into those that make a triangle and those that do not and now writes the rule.
video_script.substitution: Add the pairs that work and the pairs that fail, and compare the sums with the limit of one hundred and eighty degrees.
video_script.anchor: pairs of angles sorted into those that make a triangle and those that do not
video_script.payoff_line: Two angles make a triangle when their sum is less than one hundred and eighty degrees

final_answer.value: each angle more than 0° and the sum less than 180°; a sum of 180° or more gives no triangle
final_answer.spoken: two angles make a triangle when their sum is less than one hundred and eighty degrees, and each angle is more than zero

maths_rules: pairs that work: 70° + 30° = 100° and 90° + 85° = 175°, both less than 180°
pairs that fail: 35° + 150° = 185° and 50° + 150° = 200°, both more than 180°; and the limit pair 40° + 140° = 180° fails too
so the rule is: a triangle exists when 0° < A + B < 180° with each angle more than 0°
check: 60° + 70° = 130° is less than 180°, and the book builds a triangle with these angles
video_script.design: The pairs from the last question are shown in two columns, those that work and those that fail. Their sums are written beside them and placed on a number line with a mark at one hundred and eighty.
